newsitem.title: USA: US business economists see no recession before '99.
newsitem.headline: US business economists see no recession before '99.

text.p: The U.S. economy should be able to expand steadily with low inflation for some years yet, a 36-member panel of the National Association of Business Economists (NABE) predicted on Monday.
The business group pushed up its estimate for 1997 GDP growth to 2.6 percent from the 2.3 percent they forecast last November, but said expansion will slow to 2 percent in 1998.

"Most NABE panelists do not expect a recession before 1999, at the earliest," the group's report concluded, with most forecasting gross domestic product to grow about 2.3 percent a year between 1998 and 2002.
In the current first quarter of 1997, the NABE panelists said GDP growth likely will drop to about a 2 percent annual rate from 4.7 percent posted in the final quarter last year.

They foresaw consumer prices rising about 2.9 percent this year, the same as in 1996, and then going up 3 percent in 1998 but concluded "interest rates were likely to show little change, whether or not adjusted for inflation."

While the business economists said the Federal Reserve's monetary policy was "about right," most felt the U.S. central bank's next move would be to tighten and that the second quarter was the most likely time for an interest-rate rise.

The NABE members saw little likelihood of major improvement in the U.S. trade deficit with the rest of the world during 1997 and 1998. But they said the recent surge in the dollar's value against the yen, which complicated efforts to lower the deficit, was unlikely to continue.
"While opinion was divided, the consensus was for the dollar/yen rate to fall on balance over the next five years," the business economists said.
The economists said a balanced budget "would not benefit the economy." They urged Congress and the White House to use the same economic assumptions in drafting budget proposals.

On a separate issue, the economists criticized the government for cutting back on spending to compile federal statistics. They said businesses relied upon the data in the government reports but felt that the quality of statistical information was deteriorating.
"...Seven of 10 panel members said their analysis and decision-making were somewhat or very adversely affected by the lack of quality data," NABE reported.

It said government reports on inflation, employment and productivity were among those that most urgently needed improvement. The economists suggested combining current federal statistical activities that are scattered among departments into a new Central Statistical Office to try to improve U.S. economic data.
